title: So it isn't lost
hook: a teacher dies, his followers split, and Sariputta answers by counting

segments.voice: Yesterday: west, north, below, above, and your line, every direction. Did you honor someone who works for you? Today, a funeral, a quarrel, and a plan so it doesn't happen again. Day five hundred seventy-two.

A family group chat, a month after the grandmother's funeral. Who gets the house. Who said what at the wake. Somebody leaves the chat. Somebody posts a screenshot. The family that used to fit around one table is now three families that don't speak. The thirty-third long discourse opens with news like that. A well-known teacher of the time, Nigantha Nataputta, the teacher Jains remember as Mahavira, has just died in the town of Pava. His followers, the discourse says, have split, arguing over what he really taught, wounding each other with words. The Buddha's monks hear it. And Sariputta, his senior student, has an idea. Today: so it isn't lost.
screen: `THE GROUP CHAT AFTER THE FUNERAL.` → `A TEACHER DIES IN PAVA.` → `SARIPUTTA HAS AN IDEA.`

segments.voice: The setting is a brand-new meeting hall in Pava. The Buddha has talked with the townspeople late into the night. His back aches, so he asks Sariputta to speak to the monks while he lies down on his right side, mindful. Sariputta begins with the news from town: a community torn apart after its teacher died. Then he says, in effect: let's not let that happen to us. Let's recite the teaching together, all of us, in agreement, so that this way of life lasts long, for the good of many. And then he does what you'd do if you wanted a whole room to remember. He counts. One thing: all beings are sustained by food. Two things: name and form. Three things: the roots of harm, greed, hatred and delusion. Four: the foundations of mindfulness. On and on, all the way up to ten. The discourse is called the Sangiti Sutta, the reciting together. Remember, there were no books yet. The teaching lived in human memory, passed from mouth to ear. A list is a memory tool. A number gives the mind a shelf: if you know there are four, you notice when you've only said three. Scholars think lists like these were one way the early communities kept a huge body of teaching from drifting. And here's the quiet point. Sariputta's answer to a quarrel isn't a ruling on who was right. It's everyone saying the same words, together, out loud. At the end, the Buddha sits up and says: good, Sariputta, good.
screen: `A TEACHER DIES, A COMMUNITY SPLITS` · `LET'S RECITE IT TOGETHER` · `ONE, TWO, THREE, ALL THE WAY TO TEN` · `SAYING IT TOGETHER KEEPS THE PEACE` · then, large: `SO IT ISN'T LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one list by heart. Pick a short one. The three roots of harm: greed, hatred, delusion. Or the five precepts: no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, no intoxicants. Sit and settle. Say your list once, slowly, counting it on your fingers. Close your eyes and say it again without looking. Then let the words go and rest on the breath. If it slips away later, that's fine: that's exactly why lists come with numbers. The bell holds the time.
So it isn't lost. Sariputta's reason for reciting the teaching together: so a community stays whole, and the words outlive the people who first heard them. Today's word.
Your line: so it isn't lost. Before bed tonight, count your list on your fingers once more, or teach it to someone at the table. Day five hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Monastics in many Buddhist traditions memorize texts and chant them together, and the Pali discourses were handed down by recitation for centuries before they were written down.

fork.setup: you're Sariputta. another teacher's followers have split after his death, and the monks are uneasy. what do you do?
options: warn the monks about that other group.
recite the teaching together, number by number.
name a new leader on the spot.
fork.reveal: he proposes a common recitation, so the community agrees on the words and the teaching lasts.

original.note: Pali sangiti: reciting together. the name of DN 33, and later the word for the great councils that recited the canon.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long list of numbered teachings is a dry index.
what it means: in DN 33 it's a peace plan: everyone reciting the same words so the community doesn't split.
what a scholar hears: the Sangiti Sutta works like a memory map of the early teaching; scholars often see numbered lists like these as a seed of the later Abhidhamma.

notes: DN 33 paraphrased. Confirm the setting (the new hall of the Mallas at Pava), the Buddha's backache and his lying on his right side while Sariputta speaks.
Confirm the sample entries: ones (all beings are sustained by food), twos (name and form), threes (the three unwholesome roots), fours (the four foundations of mindfulness).

Nigantha Nataputta is traditionally identified with Mahavira of the Jains; the script reports the discourse's account of the split without judging the Jain community. A Keeper may prefer different wording.
The link between numbered lists and the Abhidhamma is a common scholarly view, stated as such.
Review edit: the hook now attributes the account of the split to the discourse (the discourse says), so it is not stated as plain history about the Jain community.
